newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: PROFILE - ING SAYS IT HAS SILENCED NAYSAYERS.
newsitem.headline: PROFILE - ING SAYS IT HAS SILENCED NAYSAYERS.

text.p: ING of the Netherlands, perhaps best known for rescuing British merchant bank Barings from collapse in 1995, prefers to present itself as tangible proof that the integrated financial services formula works.

Created as a result of a merger of NMB Postbank and insurer Nationale Nederlanden in 1991, ING says its track record since then has silenced naysayers who doubted the wisdom of marriages between banks and insurers.
"A lot of people were sceptical five years ago. Now we hardly hear any complaints," chairman Aad Jacobs told Reuters in an interview earlier this year.
Over the last five years ING's net earnings have shown average annual growth of over 17 percent and its stock market capitalisation has risen fourfold.
In terms of market value ING now ranks third among listed Dutch companies -- behind Royal Dutch Petroleum Co and Unilever NV but ahead of better know brand names such as Philips and Heineken .

Strategy has been directed towards reinforcing its positions in mature markets such as the Netherlands, the United States and Australia while building up a presence in the emerging markets of Asia, Latin American and Eastern Europe.
Tuesday's announcement of the acquisition of Equitable of Iowa confirmed analysts' expectations that ING was about to add a major U.S. life insurer to its stable of companies.
ING will take advantage of its recent New York Stock Exchange listing to pay up to 60 percent of the $2.2 billion purchase sum with ING shares which it already held.

But analysts said the deal had by no means emptied the group's warchest and that ING remained on the lookout for one or more small or medium-sized U.S. investment banks plus a significant addition to its European banking business.

ING executive board chairman Aad Jacobs acknowledged as much in a telephone interview on Tuesday, saying the group had deep pockets and was on the lookout for more opportunities to fill what it sees as gaps in its global network.
"We are a very rich company and we can afford to make a number of steps forward," he told Reuters on Tuesday.

Recently ING has given Europe a higher priority within its overall strategy, saying it wants to grab a big slice of the continent's financial services cake after the planned launch of the single European currency, the euro, in January 1999.
Jacobs said ING wanted to grow in France and Germany and has indicated that this could be achieved through cross shareholdings and alliances as well as acquisitions.
